name: Asking permission on what you own
look_for: Asking sign-off or objections on a decision inside your own ownership: "any objection?", "is that ok?", "wdyt?" at the end of a plan.
not: Review requests, and real questions where you lack the context. The stronger version states intent and keeps people informed; it never acts in silence.

refs.q: Radiating intent (instead of seeking permission or asking for forgiveness).
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path, ch. 7
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

refs.q: instead of asking permission, we would say 'I intend to...'
refs.who: L. David Marquet, Turn the Ship Around!

name: Leaving a decision open
look_for: A choice that is yours or blocks others, left without a call: "let's see", "we can decide later", options listed with no pick.
not: Asking for input before a deadline you set.

refs.q: Not deciding is a decision, usually not a good one.
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path, ch. 3
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

name: Decision not written down
look_for: A thread where you agree on something but nobody writes the decision, the owner and the reason.
not: Small calls that change nothing for others.

refs.q: Document any decision, including trade-offs and reasons.
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

name: No owner or date
look_for: Work stated with no person or day: "someone should", "we need to", "at some point".

refs.q: wrong is better than vague. Be precise about who and what will do.
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

name: Keeping work you could hand off
look_for: Taking work that would grow someone else: "I'll just do it", "faster if I do it", picking up a task a teammate asked about.
not: Hands-on work on what you lead. Staying close to some projects is part of the role.

refs.who: Will Larson, Create space for others

name: Apologising for escalating
look_for: Escalation framed as a failure or a favour: "sorry to escalate", "sorry to pull you in", or a long stuck back-and-forth with no escalation.
not: Escalations you made early and plainly; that is the strength.

refs.q: Escalations are a natural part of working together

name: Hedging a fact you know
look_for: A casual hedge before something you know: "I think maybe", "sort of", "might be wrong but", "just" on a fact.
not: Real uncertainty, real questions, and careful hedges such as "possibly" or "the data suggests". Research finds those do not hurt.

refs.says: Hedges and other powerless markers lowered ratings of the message and the speaker when readers cared about the topic.
refs.who: Blankenship & Holtgraves, 2005, J. of Language and Social Psychology

refs.says: Only casual hedges and hedges on data hurt. Professional hedges such as "possibly" did not.
refs.who: Durik et al., 2008, J. of Language and Social Psychology

name: Main point buried
look_for: The ask, the decision or the conclusion comes last, after the background.
not: Length alone. A long message with the point first is fine.

refs.q: the main point at the beginning of the correspondence
refs.who: US Army Regulation 25-50 (BLUF), quoted on Wikipedia

refs.says: Lead with the main idea, then the arguments that support it.
refs.who: Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle, via a review
refs.warn: From a review, not the book

name: Credit without names
look_for: Shipped or solved work announced with no names: "we shipped X", "I fixed Y" when others did part of it.

refs.q: amplifying – promote good work so that others know about their accomplishments
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path, ch. 8
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

refs.q: putting your thumb directly on the scale

name: Stating intent
look_for: "I'm doing X, tell me by <day> if that breaks you": you act on what you own and keep people informed.

refs.q: instead of asking permission, we would say 'I intend to...'
refs.who: L. David Marquet, Turn the Ship Around!

name: Closing with a written decision
look_for: You end a thread with the decision, the owner and the reason.

refs.q: Document any decision, including trade-offs and reasons.
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

name: Asking who cannot live with it
look_for: You check for blockers instead of agreement: "can anyone not live with this?"

refs.q: Can anyone not live with option A?
refs.who: Tanya Reilly, The Staff Engineer's Path, ch. 3
refs.warn: From a reader's notes, not the book

name: Specific praise
look_for: You name what someone did and why it mattered, not only "great job".

refs.q: Give praise that's specific and sincere

name: Naming others' work in public
look_for: You credit people by name in shared channels.

refs.q: amplifying – promote good work so that others know about their accomplishments
